report:
**Conclusion:** Extensive scientific research demonstrates that increasing the number of childhood vaccines does **not** cause autism.

**Understanding the Claim:**  
This belief stems from the "too many, too soon" hypothesis—the idea that administering multiple vaccines early in life might overwhelm an infant's immune system or trigger neurodevelopmental disorders.

**What the Evidence Shows:**  
Rigorous, peer-reviewed research has directly investigated this hypothesis and found no supporting evidence:

* **Antigen Load:** A landmark CDC study published in *The Journal of Pediatrics* measured cumulative exposure to vaccine antigens (proteins and polysaccharides that stimulate an immune response) in early childhood. Researchers found no association between the number of antigens received—either on a single day or cumulatively—and the risk of developing autism ([ScienceDaily](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2013/03/130329090310.htm); [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23545349/)).
* **Fewer Antigens Today:** Although children receive vaccines against more diseases today, advances in vaccine technology mean modern childhood immunizations expose children to significantly *fewer* total antigens than schedules used decades ago ([STAT News](https://www.statnews.com/2025/06/24/too-many-too-soon-vaccine-schedule-children-antigens-immune-system-aluminum/)).
* **Institutional Consensus:** Comprehensive reviews by the Institute of Medicine (National Academies) evaluated the safety of the recommended childhood immunization schedule and concluded that vaccines do not cause autism ([National Academies](https://www.nationalacademies.org/publications/10997)).

The idea that multiple vaccines cause autism rests on intuitive safety concerns rather than scientific data. Extensive research confirms that the childhood vaccination schedule is safe and unrelated to autism.
